prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms opened measurement of time and frequency at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B002 alone, with Katori and Ye, and I did not change my configuration between rounds. Having read the whole first round, the case has not weakened, and it has been sharpened by the objections. Six of us converge, but several moved after the openings, so I treat that as a reason to test the case harder, not as a result. The tests are these. The new element is the magic-wavelength lattice: the trapping light is tuned so that it does not shift the clock transition, which lets thousands of atoms be interrogated at once. That is a different thing from the 2005 comb, which is a ruler for optical frequencies, and from the 2012 ion work, which is control of single quantum systems. Independent confirmation is exemplary: JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, NIST, PTB and SYRTE agree at the 10^-18 level, and a systematic error in one clock would not survive that cross-comparison. It has opened new observations, namely millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, searches for varying constants and for dark matter. As an experimentalist I find the control of systematics here more convincing than for any other shortlisted instrument. The credit is the cleanest on the list: both the proposal and the realisation are carried by two people and no collaboration has to be arbitrated. The citation should rest on this demonstrated physics and not on the pending redefinition of the second.
statement.case_against: The real objection is Mehlig's: is this a discovery about nature or a precision technology in a lineage the Academy has already honoured (Hall and Hansch 2005, Wineland and Haroche 2012, with Ye in the first)? My answer is that the statute allows an invention that gives physics a new capability, but only when the use is demonstrated, and here it is. I accept this is a judgement of weight and not a fact, and Mehlig's low ranking is a legitimate dissent. Second, priority and division of credit between Katori (proposal and first Sr lattice clock) and Ye (accuracy and stability records) is something I cannot check from my own field. I rely on Lindroth, Kroll and Olsson for the chronology, and I note that no member has reported that check yet. If the chronology showed parallel claimants with equal standing, the exact pair would need reopening. Third, a clock prize competes with IceCube (B043), which is a first observation of a new astrophysical flux, and with the Higgs experiments (B053), which are the larger discovery. B053 stays outside my preferred configuration only because I still cannot defend a rule-compliant three-name credit.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether the prize should go to the original experiment (Katori) and not to the later, more accurate realisation (Ye), and wants the priority record checked before accepting the pair.
responses.response: I share your criterion, and I think it supports the pair and not Katori alone. As I read the record, which I cannot verify from my own field, the lattice scheme and the first strontium lattice clock come from Katori's group in Tokyo, whereas the demonstrations that made lattice clocks a precision instrument for redshift and constants, with a very different stability, come from Ye's group. Dropping Ye would honour the idea and leave out the work that made the field believe it, which is the confirmation I ask for. I will not claim the chronology is settled, and I ask that Lindroth or Kroll confirm it from the original papers before the ballot. If it holds, the citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice and the many-atom regime, so that the first-experiment criterion is visibly met.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B002 eighth because the 2005 and 2012 prizes already cover time metrology, and he asks whether a clock is conceptually new enough.
responses.response: This is the strongest opposing view and I do not dismiss it. I would separate the subject, which is time metrology in all three prizes, from the content recognised. In 2005 it was the comb as a frequency ruler, in 2012 control of single trapped quantum systems. Neither solved the problem that Katori solved, namely trapping many atoms in light without moving the transition, and the gain is statistical, since many atoms beat the projection-noise limit of a single ion. I also note that the same logic applied to your KPZ preference, which I find mature, only goes to show that conceptual centrality and instrument capability are different tests. We weigh them differently, and I would rather say that openly than pretend we agree.

responses.point: Lindroth says the citation must state the difference from the comb and ion prizes, and asks whether the credited pair should be widened because Lemonde, Derevianko and the Sr and Yb communities also contributed.
responses.response: Agreed on the wording. I would not widen the pair. The cap is three, and adding a third name from the wider community would require a priority finding that no one has made and would dilute a credit that is clean as it stands. If the chronology check you and Kroll are being asked to do shows a parallel proposal of equal standing, then I would revisit, but I do not want to add a name on the suspicion alone. Your point on cross-laboratory comparison is the one I would put first in the case, and I have done so above.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B015 as a new state of matter confirmed in HgTe, InAs/GaSb and 3D materials, and asks the committee to weigh a state of matter against a measurement capability.
responses.response: I take the emphasis question seriously. The physics of topological insulators is mature and the independent confirmation is excellent, and I outside my field cannot fault it. Where I cannot follow is attribution. By your own account Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang (deceased) and the 3D contributors fall outside Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, and the 2016 prize overlaps in subject. The chair's question is whether a defensible three-name credit exists, and I do not think it does without a framing that the other members have called contestable. That is why B015 is not in my configuration, although I would not oppose it if the credit were resolved differently.

responses.point: Danielsson now prefers B002 but says the Higgs experiments remain the larger discovery and that his move may favour the comfortable attribution over the important discovery.
responses.response: I understand the worry, and I share it in part since I started in particle physics. But the statute asks for the decisive contribution, and for B053 I still cannot say that spokespersons and founders were that. A prize that rewards detector leadership is a defensible theory, but it would have to be stated openly in the citation and I do not think the committee has reached it. So I do not think you chose the comfortable option. You chose the one where the credit can be defended line by line, which is also what I tell myself on B043, where the diffuse flux is secure but the pioneers are uncredited.

uncertainties: The chronology of the magic-wavelength proposal and of the first lattice-clock demonstrations (Katori, Ye, and parallel proposals such as Lemonde's) has not been confirmed by any member against the original papers, and it could change the exact pair.
Whether the committee as a whole accepts the lattice clock as a distinct discovery or capability and not as a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 prizes, where Mehlig dissents.

Whether a rule-compliant, defensible three-person credit for the Higgs observation or for IceCube (with the DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA pioneers) could be stated, which would change my ranking of B053 and B043 relative to B002.
Whether a second part would strengthen the prize at all, since the cap of three people leaves room for only one name beside Katori and Ye and no candidate fits that slot.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with B002. I am a member of PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur and work in astroparticle physics, so I am close to B043 and to antimatter work such as B063, and I trained at CERN, near B053. I have no collaboration with any named shortlisted candidate, and no change since round 1. As Chair I am also steering the process, so I rely on the other members for the atomic-physics priority question.
